== PART I: ENGLISH ==

== Section 1: Stocks — The Foundation of All Cooking ==
Stock is the backbone of professional cooking. It is the liquid foundation upon which sauces, soups, braises, and reductions are built. The French word for stock is fond, meaning "foundation" or "base," reflecting its central importance in cuisine. Auguste Escoffier, the father of modern French cooking, considered stock-making the single most important skill a chef could master.
The Master Stock Formula
1 Gallon of Stock = 8 Lbs of Bones + 6 Quarts of Water + 1 Lb Mirepoix
Key Rule: Add herbs and mirepoix during the last hour of cooking for maximum flavor retention. Adding aromatics too early causes their volatile compounds to evaporate during the long simmer.
Cooking Times by Bone Type
Stock Type
Time
Notes
Poultry Stock
4–6 Hours
Chicken, turkey, or duck bones
Veal Stock
6–8 Hours
Produces rich gelatin body
Beef Stock
8–12 Hours
Hearty, deep flavor
Fish/Shellfish (Fumet)
30–45 Minutes
Overcooking creates bitterness
Vegetable Stock
45–60 Minutes
No bones; delicate

Brown Stock vs. White Stock
Brown Stock: Bones are roasted at 400°F (200°C) before simmering. Roasting caramelizes proteins and sugars on the bone surfaces through the Maillard reaction, producing deep color and rich, complex flavor. Tomato paste is often added to the roasting pan for additional depth. Used for Espagnole sauce and demi-glace.
White Stock: Bones are NOT roasted. They are blanched briefly in boiling water, then rinsed and placed directly in cold water to simmer. This produces a lighter, more neutral liquid. Used for Velouté sauce, cream soups, and delicate preparations.
Mirepoix
Mirepoix is the aromatic vegetable base of French cooking:
50% Onion + 25% Carrot + 25% Celery
For white stocks, a "white mirepoix" omits carrot (which adds color) and substitutes leek, parsnip, or additional celery.

== Section 2: Thickening Agents ==
Roux
A roux is equal parts fat (usually butter) and flour, cooked together in a pan. The cooking time determines the color and flavor:
White Roux: Cooked 2–3 minutes. Mild flavor, maximum thickening power. Used for Béchamel.
Blond Roux: Cooked 4–5 minutes. Nutty aroma. Used for Velouté.
Brown Roux: Cooked 8–15 minutes. Deep color, reduced thickening power. Used for Espagnole and gumbo.
Roux can also be made with stock instead of butter as the liquid component, though butter is traditional.
Cornstarch Slurry
Equal Parts Cornstarch and Cold Water, whisked together until smooth, then added to hot liquid while stirring. Always add slurry to hot liquid, never the reverse. The starch granules swell and burst upon contact with heat, creating thickening. Cornstarch produces a glossy, translucent finish compared to the opaque finish of flour-based roux.

Other Thickening Methods
Liaison: Egg yolks tempered with cream, used to finish velouté and cream soups
Beurre Manié: Equal parts softened butter and flour kneaded together, whisked into hot liquid at the end
Reduction: Simply boiling liquid to evaporate water, concentrating flavors and thickening naturally

== Section 3: The Five French Mother Sauces ==
The five mother sauces (sauces mères) were codified by Marie-Antoine Carême in the early 19th century and later refined by Auguste Escoffier. Every classical French sauce derives from one of these five foundations. Mastery of the mother sauces is considered the gateway to mastery of all sauces.

# Béchamel — The White Sauce
Formula: Milk, boiled and reduced, then thickened with white roux.
Béchamel is the simplest mother sauce. Milk is heated (often infused with onion, bay leaf, and nutmeg), then a white roux is whisked in to create a smooth, creamy sauce. It is the base for macaroni and cheese, lasagna, croque madame, and gratins.
Daughter sauces: Mornay (add Gruyère cheese), Cream Sauce (add heavy cream), Mustard Sauce (add Dijon mustard), Nantua (add crayfish butter).
# Velouté — The Velvety Sauce
Formula: White stock (chicken, veal, or fish), boiled and reduced, then thickened with blond roux or cornstarch slurry.
Velouté means "velvety" in French. It should be silky smooth and light. The stock used determines the name: chicken velouté, fish velouté, etc.
Daughter sauces: Allemande (add egg yolk and lemon), Suprême (add cream and mushroom), Normande (add egg, butter, cream), White Wine Sauce.
# Sauce Tomat — The Tomato Sauce
Formula: Mirepoix base (without avocado or cilantro, like the base of guacamole), combined with tomato paste and stock.
The classical French sauce tomat is not Italian marinara. It traditionally includes salted pork belly, mirepoix, garlic, white stock, and tomato purée, sometimes thickened with roux. Modern adaptations often simplify to tomatoes, olive oil, garlic, and herbs.
Daughter sauces: Creole Sauce (add bell peppers, celery, spice), Provençal (add basil, fennel, rosemary), Portuguese Sauce (add onions, garlic, parsley).
# Hollandaise — The Emulsion Sauce
Formula: Thickened butter using egg yolks, water, and acid (lemon juice or white wine vinegar).
Hollandaise is an emulsion sauce, not thickened by roux but by the suspension of clarified butter droplets within egg yolks. The egg yolks act as emulsifiers. It is notoriously tricky — too much heat scrambles the eggs; too little fails to emulsify. It must be served immediately and cannot be reheated.
Daughter sauces: Béarnaise (add tarragon and shallot), Choron (add tomato), Maltaise (add blood orange juice), Mousseline (fold in whipped cream).
# Espagnole — The Brown Sauce
Formula: Brown veal stock with additional mirepoix, tomato pincé (tomato paste cooked until brick-red), and aromatics, thickened by boiling with brown roux.
Espagnole is the most complex mother sauce, requiring brown stock (from roasted bones), brown roux, tomato paste, and hours of simmering and skimming. It is rarely served on its own but reduced further into demi-glace (half Espagnole, half brown stock, reduced by half).
Daughter sauces: Demi-Glace (the king of all sauces), Bordelaise (add red wine, shallots, bone marrow), Chasseur/Hunter’s Sauce (add mushrooms, tomato, white wine), Robert (add mustard, onion).

== Section 4: Cooking Methods ==
Method
Description
Poach
Cook gently in liquid at 160–180°F. Barely simmering, no bubbles breaking the surface. Used for eggs, fish, chicken.
Shallow Poach
Food is half submerged in liquid. Covered with parchment (cartouche). Used for delicate fish fillets.
Sauté
Cook quickly in a small amount of fat over high heat. Food must be dry. Pan must be hot. Don’t crowd the pan.
Fry (Deep Fry)
Fully submerge food in hot fat (350–375°F). Creates crispy exterior while cooking interior through.
Braise
Sear food in hot fat, then simmer in fat or other liquid in a covered vessel, often finished in an oven. Low and slow.
Roast
Cook with dry heat in an oven, on a pan, or by smoking. Includes baking and smoke-roasting.
Temper
Adding a hot liquid slowly to a cold mixture (or vice versa) to gradually equalize temperature without shocking.

Tempering in Practice: When making Hollandaise, you temper the hot clarified butter into the egg yolks drop by drop. When adding a liaison to soup, you temper the hot soup into the egg-cream mixture first, then return it to the pot. This prevents scrambling.

== Section 5: Emulsions and The Creaming Method ==
Emulsions
An emulsion is a stable mixture of two liquids that normally don’t combine (like oil and water). An emulsifier (such as egg yolk, mustard, or lecithin) is needed to bind them. In cooking, emulsions include Hollandaise, mayonnaise, vinaigrettes, and cream sauces. There are two types:
Oil-in-water: Oil droplets suspended in water (vinaigrette, milk)
Water-in-oil: Water droplets suspended in oil (butter, margarine)
The Creaming Method
The creaming method is a baking technique where butter and sugar are beaten together until light and fluffy, incorporating air. This aeration is the primary leavening mechanism in pound cakes, butter cakes, and cookies.
Classic Pound Cake (The 1:1:1:1 Formula)
1 Pound Flour + 1 Pound Sugar + 1 Pound Butter + 1 Pound Eggs + Flavorings
This equal-weight formula dates to 18th century England. The name "pound cake" comes directly from the recipe. Modern variations may adjust ratios, add baking powder, or incorporate sour cream for moisture.

== Section 6: Specific Cookery Topics ==
Potato Cookery
Potatoes are classified by starch content: high-starch (Russet/Idaho, best for baking and frying), medium-starch (Yukon Gold, all-purpose), and low-starch/waxy (Red, Fingerling, best for boiling and salads). High starch potatoes become fluffy when cooked; waxy potatoes hold their shape.
Rice Cookery
The standard absorption method uses a 2:1 water-to-rice ratio for long grain white rice. Rice should be rinsed until water runs clear to remove excess surface starch. The pilaf method toasts rice in fat before adding liquid, creating separate, fluffy grains.
Pasta
Fresh pasta is made from flour and eggs (typically 100g flour per egg). Dried pasta is made from semolina and water. Cook in heavily salted water ("like the sea"). Reserve pasta water — the starchy liquid is the secret to binding sauces to noodles.
Vegetable Cookery
The key principle: don’t overcook. Blanch green vegetables in boiling salted water, then shock in ice water to preserve color and texture. Root vegetables start in cold water. This ensures even cooking from the outside in.
Egg Cookery
Eggs are one of the most versatile ingredients in cooking. They leaven (soufflés), thicken (custards), emulsify (hollandaise), bind (meatloaf), clarify (consommé), and coat (breading). Temperature control is everything with eggs — they begin to set at 144°F and are fully firm at 180°F.
Plating
Plating is the art of food presentation. Classical plating uses the "clock method" — protein at 6 o’clock, starch at 10, vegetable at 2. Modern plating emphasizes odd numbers, height, negative space, sauce as art, and the rim as a frame. Wipe the rim clean before service.
Knife Skills
The foundation of all kitchen work. The four essential cuts: brunoise (1/8" dice), small dice (1/4"), medium dice (1/2"), and large dice (3/4"). The julienne is 1/8" x 1/8" x 2–3" matchsticks. Chiffonade is finely sliced leafy herbs. A sharp knife is safer than a dull one.
Steps of Service (Front of House)
Steps of Service is the structured sequence of guest interaction in a restaurant: greeting and seating, beverage order, appetizer order, entrée order, food delivery and check-back, table maintenance, dessert and after-dinner service, check presentation, and farewell. Understanding both BOH and FOH creates a complete hospitality professional.

== Section 7: Recipes ==
Butter Bars (Gooey Butter Cake Bars)
1 box (18.25 oz) yellow cake mix
1/2 cup butter, melted
4 large eggs, divided
8 ounces cream cheese, softened
4 cups powdered sugar
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
Bottom layer: Mix cake mix, melted butter, and 1 egg. Press into greased 9x13 pan. Top layer: Beat cream cheese, remaining 3 eggs, powdered sugar, and vanilla until smooth. Pour over bottom layer. Bake 350°F for 40–45 minutes until golden and set around edges but slightly gooey in center.
Au Gratin Potatoes
1 1/2 cups full-fat cream
2 garlic cloves, minced
2 tbsp unsalted butter, melted
2.5 lb starchy potatoes (Russet), sliced thin
1 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp pepper
2 1/2 cups Gruyère cheese, freshly grated (or colby, cheddar, havarti)
2 tsp fresh thyme leaves (optional but recommended)
Method: Preheat 375°F. Rub baking dish with butter. Layer sliced potatoes, seasoning each layer with salt, pepper, thyme, and cheese. Combine cream and garlic, pour over potatoes. Top with remaining cheese. Cover with foil, bake 60 min. Remove foil, bake 15–20 min more until golden and bubbling.
Simple Homemade Biscuits
2 cups all-purpose flour
1 tablespoon baking powder
1 teaspoon sugar
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/3 cup cold butter (frozen is best)
3/4 cup cold milk or buttermilk
Method: Preheat 425°F. Whisk dry ingredients. Grate frozen butter into flour, toss to combine. Add cold milk, stir until just combined — do not overmix. Turn onto floured surface, fold dough 5–6 times for flaky layers. Pat to 3/4" thick. Cut with biscuit cutter (press straight down, don’t twist). Place touching on baking sheet. Bake 12–15 minutes until golden. Brush with melted butter immediately.
Simple Homemade Brownies
1/2 cup (1 stick) butter, melted
1 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1/3 cup unsweetened cocoa powder
1/2 cup all-purpose flour
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/4 teaspoon baking powder
Method: Preheat 350°F. Line 8x8 pan with parchment. Whisk melted butter and sugar. Add eggs and vanilla, whisk vigorously 2 minutes (this creates the crinkly top). Fold in cocoa, flour, salt, and baking powder until just combined. Spread into pan. Bake 25–30 minutes. Do not overbake — a toothpick should come out with moist crumbs, not wet batter.
Cannabis Oil Brownies
Note: This recipe uses cannabis-infused cooking oil prepared through lipid extraction. Cannabis is legally available in many jurisdictions for medical or adult use. Always comply with local laws.
Cannabis Oil Preparation (Decarboxylation + Lipid Extraction): Decarboxylation converts inactive THCA to active THC. Grind cannabis, spread on baking sheet, bake at 240°F for 40 minutes (low and slow to avoid burning terpenes). Combine decarboxylated cannabis with coconut oil or butter at a ratio of approximately 1 oz flower per 1 cup oil. Simmer at 160–180°F for 2–3 hours (never boil). Strain through cheesecloth. The resulting oil can be used 1:1 as a substitute in any recipe calling for butter or oil.
Brownie Modification: Follow the brownie recipe above, substituting cannabis-infused butter for regular butter. Start with half the infused oil if dosage is unknown. Effects take 45–90 minutes to onset and can last 4–8 hours. Always label clearly and store safely.

== Section 8: The Oilahuasca Principle ==
The term "Oilahuasca" was coined by researcher Ron69 (69Ron) on the HerbPedia Wikidot. It is a portmanteau of "oil" and "ayahuasca," referencing the parallel principle of enzyme manipulation. Just as ayahuasca uses monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) to render DMT orally active, Oilahuasca uses CYP450 enzyme inhibitors and inducers to modify how the human body metabolizes allylbenzene compounds found in common culinary spices.
The Core Theory
Common kitchen spices contain allylbenzene compounds: myristicin (nutmeg), elemicin (nutmeg), safrole (sassafras), methyl chavicol (basil), eugenol (clove), and others. These compounds are metabolized by Cytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver. Under normal circumstances, most allylbenzenes are rapidly deactivated. However, by selectively inhibiting certain CYP450 enzymes while inducing others, the metabolic pathway can be redirected toward the formation of psychoactive alkaloid adducts.
Key CYP450 Enzymes
Enzymes to INDUCE (activate allylbenzenes): CYP2A6, CYP2C9, CYP2E1, and sometimes CYP1A2. These enzymes help convert allylbenzenes to their 1′-hydroxylated alcohol intermediates.
Enzymes to INHIBIT (prevent deactivation): CYP2D6, CYP3A4, and sometimes CYP1A2. Inhibiting these prevents premature metabolic breakdown.
Critical enzyme — 17bHSD2: This enzyme converts the 1′-hydroxy intermediates into phenyl vinyl ketones, which then spontaneously condense with endogenous amines (dimethylamine, piperidine, pyrrolidine) to form alkaloid metabolites. If 17bHSD2 is inhibited (e.g., by naringenin in grapefruit), allylbenzenes cannot produce psychoactive effects.
The Coffee Connection
"Some people have reported psychedelic effects from mixing just coffee, almond, cinnamon, vanilla and nutmeg." — HerbPedia / Oilahuasca Forum
Coffee is a powerful CYP1A2 inducer — it increases the body’s production of this enzyme. When cinnamon and nutmeg then inhibit the enlarged CYP1A2 pool, the result is greater accumulation of active intermediates. The bigger the enzyme system, the greater the potential for accumulation when blocked. This is the same principle behind pharmaceutical warnings about grapefruit juice and medication interactions.

The Betel Quid: The Original Oilahuasca
The betel quid — chewed by approximately 600 million people worldwide — is perhaps the oldest and most widespread example of the Oilahuasca principle in practice. The traditional three-component formula (areca nut + betel leaf + slaked lime) demonstrates sophisticated enzymatic knowledge: the areca nut provides the psychoactive arecoline, the betel leaf provides CYP450-modulating chavibetol, and the slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) adjusts pH to optimize bioavailability. This is enzyme manipulation encoded in cultural practice.
Historical Context: Shulgin’s Ten Essential Oils
Alexander Shulgin, in PiHKAL, listed allylbenzene compounds found in common spice oils and noted that they were structurally related to known psychoactive phenethylamines. He theorized that these compounds might be "aminized" by the body’s own enzymes to form active metabolites. This was the theoretical predecessor to Ron69’s practical Oilahuasca work. The key insight: your spice cabinet contains the precursors; your liver contains the laboratory.

== Section 9: Cannabis Oil Extraction and MHRB Cold Water Preparation ==
Cannabis Oil Extraction: The Lipid Method
Cannabis extraction into cooking oil follows the same fundamental chemistry as stock-making and sauce-making: dissolving flavor and active compounds into a carrier medium. THC and other cannabinoids are lipophilic (fat-soluble), meaning they dissolve readily into fats and oils but poorly into water. This is why traditional Indian Bhang preparation uses milk and ghee, and why modern edibles use butter or coconut oil.
The Process
Step 1 — Decarboxylation: Raw cannabis contains THCA (tetrahydrocannabinolic acid), which is not psychoactive. Heat converts THCA to THC through decarboxylation. Grind cannabis coarsely, spread on a parchment-lined baking sheet, and bake at 240°F (115°C) for 40 minutes.
Step 2 — Lipid Extraction: Combine decarboxylated cannabis with coconut oil, butter, or olive oil (approximately 1 oz flower per 1 cup oil). Heat at 160–180°F (70–82°C) for 2–3 hours. Never boil — high temperatures degrade THC into CBN (sedative). A slow cooker on “warm” or a double boiler works well.
Step 3 — Filtration: Strain through cheesecloth or fine mesh into a jar. Squeeze to extract maximum oil. Discard plant material. The resulting infused oil can be used as a 1:1 replacement in any recipe calling for butter or oil.
The CYP450 Connection
Cannabis shares enzyme interaction principles with Oilahuasca. Black pepper (piperine) inhibits CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, increasing bioavailability of cannabinoids by up to 2000%. This is the same principle used in Indian Trikatu formulations for millennia, and is why traditional Bhang preparations often include black pepper.
MHRB Cold Water Extraction
Mimosa hostilis root bark (MHRB), also known as Mimosa tenuiflora, contains DMT (N,N-Dimethyltryptamine) and other tryptamines. Traditionally used in Brazilian Jurema ceremonies.
Cold Water Method (Cold Brew Jurema)
Inspired by traditional Brazilian preparation and validated by ethnobotanist Jonathan Ott’s self-experiments, the cold water extraction involves soaking finely powdered MHRB in cold water in a refrigerator for an extended period (several hours to overnight). The liquid is strained and consumed. The resulting brew is characteristically deep purple.
The Yuremamine Mystery
In 2005, researchers isolated a novel compound called yuremamine from Mimosa tenuiflora. Yuremamine may explain why cold water Jurema preparations appear to be psychoactive without added MAOIs — something that should be pharmacologically impossible since gut MAO normally degrades DMT before absorption. Yuremamine appears to be heat-sensitive, meaning it is destroyed by boiling but preserved in cold water extraction. This remains an active area of research.
The Cooking Oil Method (Lime + Oil Tek)
DMT in MHRB exists in acid salt form. Food-grade calcium hydroxide (pickling lime) is mixed with powdered bark and minimal water to create a paste, converting DMT to its freebase form. Cooking oil is then added as a non-polar solvent to absorb the freebased DMT. The oil is separated and can be consumed directly or in food. Every substance used is edible — a significant safety advantage over traditional crystalline extraction methods that use caustic lye and flammable naphtha.
Safety Note: DMT is a controlled substance in most jurisdictions. MAOI interactions with SSRIs and many other medications can cause potentially fatal serotonin syndrome. This information is presented for educational and harm reduction purposes. Always consult local laws and medical professionals.

TEIL II: DEUTSCH

== Abschnitt 1: Fond — Die Grundlage des Kochens ==
Fond ist das Rückgrat der professionellen Küche. Er ist die flüssige Grundlage, auf der Saucen, Suppen, Schmorbrühen und Reduktionen aufgebaut werden. Auguste Escoffier, der Vater der modernen französischen Küche, betrachtete die Fondherstellung als die wichtigste Fähigkeit, die ein Koch beherrschen kann.
Die Grundformel
1 Gallone Fond = 8 Pfund Knochen + 6 Quart Wasser + 1 Pfund Mirepoix
Wichtige Regel: Kräuter und Mirepoix erst in der letzten Stunde hinzufügen, um maximalen Geschmack zu erhalten.
Kochzeiten nach Knochenart
Geflügelfond: 4–6 Stunden
Kalbsfond: 6–8 Stunden
Brauner Fond: Geröstete Knochen (Maillard-Reaktion für tiefe Farbe und Geschmack)
Weißer Fond: Nicht geröstete Knochen (hell, neutral)
Mirepoix
50% Zwiebel + 25% Karotte + 25% Sellerie
Mehlschwitze (Roux)
Butter und Mehl zu gleichen Teilen, in einer Pfanne zusammen gekocht. Weiße Mehlschwitze (2–3 Min.), Blonde Mehlschwitze (4–5 Min.), Braune Mehlschwitze (8–15 Min.).
Stärkebinder
Maisstärke-Aufschlämmung: Gleiche Teile Maisstärke und kaltes Wasser.

== Abschnitt 2: Die fünf französischen Grundsaucen ==
Die fünf Grundsaucen (sauces mères) wurden von Marie-Antoine Carême klassifiziert und später von Auguste Escoffier verfeinert.
# Béchamel — Die Weiße Sauce
Formel: Milch, aufgekocht und reduziert, dann mit weißer Mehlschwitze angedickt.
# Velouté — Die Samtige Sauce
Formel: Weißer Fond, aufgekocht und reduziert, dann mit blonder Mehlschwitze oder Maisstärke angedickt.
# Sauce Tomat — Die Tomatensauce
Formel: Mirepoix-Basis mit Tomatenmark und Fond.
# Hollandaise — Die Emulsionssauce
Formel: Eingedickte Butter mit Eigelb, Wasser und Säure (Zitronensaft oder Weißweinessig).
# Espagnole — Die Braune Sauce
Formel: Brauner Kalbsfond mit zusätzlichem Mirepoix, Tomaten-Pincé und Gewürzen, mit brauner Mehlschwitze angedickt.

== Abschnitt 3: Kochmethoden ==
Pochieren: Sanft in Flüssigkeit garen bei 70–82°C
Flach Pochieren: Halb eingetaucht in Flüssigkeit
Sautieren: Schnell in wenig Fett bei hoher Hitze braten
Frittieren: Vollständig in heißem Fett untertauchen
Schmoren: In heißem Fett anbraten, dann in Flüssigkeit in geschlossenem Gefäß langsam garen
Braten/Rösten: Trockene Hitze im Ofen, in der Pfanne oder Räuchern
Temperieren: Langsames Hinzufügen von heißer zu kalter Flüssigkeit

== Abschnitt 4: Rezepte ==
Einfache Butterkekse (Biscuits)
2 Tassen Mehl, 1 EL Backpulver, 1 TL Zucker, 1/2 TL Salz, 1/3 Tasse kalte Butter (gefroren am besten), 3/4 Tasse kalte Milch. Ofen auf 220°C vorheizen. Trockene Zutaten mischen. Gefrorene Butter hineinreiben. Kalte Milch hinzufügen, kurz verrühren. 5–6 Mal falten. 2 cm dick ausrollen. Ausstechen. 12–15 Minuten backen.
Einfache Brownies
1/2 Tasse geschmolzene Butter, 1 Tasse Zucker, 2 Eier, 1 TL Vanille, 1/3 Tasse Kakaopulver, 1/2 Tasse Mehl, 1/4 TL Salz, 1/4 TL Backpulver. Ofen auf 175°C. Butter und Zucker verrühren. Eier und Vanille dazu, 2 Minuten kräftig schlagen. Trockene Zutaten unterheben. In 20x20 cm Form. 25–30 Minuten backen.
Cannabis-Öl-Brownies
Cannabis-Öl-Herstellung: Cannabis bei 115°C 40 Minuten decarboxylieren. Mit Kokosöl bei 70–82°C 2–3 Stunden extrahieren. Abseihen. Das infundierte Öl kann 1:1 als Butterersatz verwendet werden.

== Abschnitt 5: Das Oilahuasca-Prinzip ==
Der Begriff "Oilahuasca" wurde von dem Forscher Ron69 auf HerbPedia geprägt. Es ist ein Kofferwort aus "Öl" und "Ayahuasca". Gewöhnliche Küchengewürze enthalten Allylbenzol-Verbindungen: Myristicin (Muskatnuss), Elemicin (Muskatnuss), Safrol (Sassafras), Methylchavicol (Basilikum), Eugenol (Nelke). Durch selektive Hemmung bestimmter CYP450-Enzyme bei gleichzeitiger Induktion anderer kann der Stoffwechselweg in Richtung psychoaktiver Alkaloid-Addukte umgeleitet werden.
"Einige Menschen haben über psychedelische Wirkungen berichtet, wenn sie nur Kaffee, Mandel, Zimt, Vanille und Muskatnuss mischten." — HerbPedia / Oilahuasca-Forum
MHRB Kaltwasser-Extraktion
Mimosa-hostilis-Wurzelrinde wird fein gemahlen und in kaltem Wasser im Kühlschrank über mehrere Stunden eingeweicht. Die Flüssigkeit wird abgeseiht und konsumiert. Die resultierende Brühe ist charakteristisch tiefviolett. Im Jahr 2005 isolierten Forscher eine neuartige Verbindung namens Yuremamin aus Mimosa tenuiflora, die möglicherweise erklärt, warum Kaltwasser-Jurema-Zubereitungen ohne zugesetzte MAOIs psychoaktiv zu sein scheinen.

PARTE III: ITALIANO

== Sezione 1: Il Brodo — Le Fondamenta della Cucina ==
Il brodo è la spina dorsale della cucina professionale. È la base liquida su cui si costruiscono salse, zuppe, brasati e riduzioni. La parola francese per brodo è "fond", che significa "fondamento", riflettendo la sua importanza centrale nella cucina.
La Formula Base
1 Gallone di Brodo = 8 Libbre di Ossa + 6 Quarti d’Acqua + 1 Libbra di Mirepoix
Regola Chiave: Aggiungere erbe e mirepoix nell’ultima ora di cottura per il massimo sapore.
Tempi di Cottura
Brodo di Pollame: 4–6 Ore
Brodo di Vitello: 6–8 Ore
Brodo Scuro: Ossa arrostite (reazione di Maillard per colore e sapore profondi)
Brodo Bianco: Ossa non arrostite (chiaro, neutro)
Mirepoix
50% Cipolla + 25% Carota + 25% Sedano
Roux
Parti uguali di burro e farina, cotti insieme in padella. Roux bianco (2–3 min), Roux biondo (4–5 min), Roux scuro (8–15 min).
Addensante di Amido
Impasto di Amido di Mais: Parti uguali di amido di mais e acqua fredda.

== Sezione 2: Le Cinque Salse Madri Francesi ==
Le cinque salse madri (sauces mères) furono codificate da Marie-Antoine Carême e successivamente perfezionate da Auguste Escoffier.
# Besciamella — La Salsa Bianca
Formula: Latte, portato a ebollizione e ridotto, poi addensato con roux bianco.
# Velouté — La Salsa Vellutata
Formula: Brodo bianco, portato a ebollizione e ridotto, poi addensato con roux biondo o amido di mais.
# Salsa di Pomodoro
Formula: Base di mirepoix con concentrato di pomodoro e brodo.
# Olandese — La Salsa Emulsionata
Formula: Burro addensato con tuorli d’uovo, acqua e acido (succo di limone o aceto di vino bianco).
# Spagnola — La Salsa Scura
Formula: Brodo scuro di vitello con mirepoix aggiuntivo, concentrato di pomodoro e aromi, addensato con roux scuro.

== Sezione 3: Metodi di Cottura ==
Affogare: Cuocere delicatamente in liquido a 70–82°C
Affogatura Superficiale: Cibo mezzo immerso nel liquido
Saltare: Cuocere rapidamente in poco grasso a fuoco alto
Friggere: Immergere completamente nel grasso caldo
Brasare: Rosolare nel grasso caldo, poi cuocere a fuoco lento in liquido in recipiente coperto
Arrostire: Calore secco nel forno, in padella o affumicatura
Temperare: Aggiungere lentamente liquido caldo a miscela fredda

== Sezione 4: Ricette ==
Biscotti Semplici Fatti in Casa
2 tazze di farina, 1 cucchiaio di lievito in polvere, 1 cucchiaino di zucchero, 1/2 cucchiaino di sale, 1/3 tazza di burro freddo (congelato è meglio), 3/4 tazza di latte freddo. Preriscaldare il forno a 220°C. Mescolare gli ingredienti secchi. Grattugiare il burro congelato nella farina. Aggiungere il latte freddo, mescolare brevemente. Piegare 5–6 volte. Stendere a 2 cm di spessore. Tagliare. Cuocere 12–15 minuti.
Brownies Semplici
1/2 tazza di burro fuso, 1 tazza di zucchero, 2 uova, 1 cucchiaino di vaniglia, 1/3 tazza di cacao in polvere, 1/2 tazza di farina, 1/4 cucchiaino di sale, 1/4 cucchiaino di lievito. Forno a 175°C. Mescolare burro e zucchero. Aggiungere uova e vaniglia, sbattere vigorosamente per 2 minuti. Incorporare gli ingredienti secchi. Versare in teglia 20x20 cm. Cuocere 25–30 minuti.
Brownies all’Olio di Cannabis
Preparazione dell’Olio di Cannabis: Decarbossilare la cannabis a 115°C per 40 minuti. Estrarre con olio di cocco a 70–82°C per 2–3 ore. Filtrare. L’olio infuso può essere usato come sostituto 1:1 del burro.

== Sezione 5: Il Principio dell’Oilahuasca ==
Il termine "Oilahuasca" è stato coniato dal ricercatore Ron69 su HerbPedia. È un neologismo che unisce "óleo" (olio) e "ayahuasca". Le spezie da cucina comuni contengono composti allilbenzenici: miristicina (noce moscata), elemicina (noce moscata), safrolo (sassafrasso), metilcavicolo (basilico), eugenolo (chiodi di garofano). Inibendo selettivamente alcuni enzimi CYP450 e inducendone altri, la via metabolica può essere reindirizzata verso la formazione di addotti alcaloidi psicoattivi.
"Alcune persone hanno riportato effetti psichedelici mescolando semplicemente caffè, mandorla, cannella, vaniglia e noce moscata." — HerbPedia / Forum Oilahuasca
Estrazione MHRB con Acqua Fredda
La corteccia di radice di Mimosa hostilis viene finemente macinata e messa in ammollo in acqua fredda in frigorifero per diverse ore. Il liquido viene filtrato e consumato. La bevanda risultante è caratteristicamente di colore viola intenso. Nel 2005, i ricercatori hanno isolato un nuovo composto chiamato yuremamina dalla Mimosa tenuiflora, che potrebbe spiegare perché le preparazioni fredde di Jurema sembrano essere psicoattive senza IMAO aggiunti.
